forces: Flute, solo violin, obbligato harpsichord, strings and continuo
performers: Advent Chamber Orchestra; Roxana Pavel Goldstein, violin; Constance Schoepflin, flute; Matthew Ganong, harpsichord
question: How does a dance rhythm remain recognisable inside imitative counterpoint?
intro: A gigue-like figure becomes a subject for imitation, first among the soloists and then across the ensemble. The broad design is a returning opening section around a longer middle span, not another first-movement cadenza.

sections.label: A · Fugal opening in D major
sections.mNote: solo entries grow into ensemble counterpoint

sections.label: B · Minor-key episodes
sections.mNote: the opening figure continues through changing keys and textures

sections.label: A′ · Opening section returns
sections.mNote: the opening imitations and D-major ensemble writing return

cues.title: A dance becomes counterpoint
cues.text: The violin begins a figure that the flute and keyboard take up in turn. Its dotted start and running triplets give the imitation a dance pulse: several lines can overlap without losing the same rhythmic character.
cues.evidence: The opening of the BGA full score, printed p. 152, shows the successive solo entries and triplet figure. The note describes the opening stretch, not their individual entrance times.

cues.title: Two beats, three subdivisions
cues.text: The score is in 2/4, but triplets divide many beats into three. Listen for the two larger pulses underneath the small running notes; the larger beat keeps the contrapuntal entries connected to a gigue-like dance.
cues.evidence: The 2/4 signature and triplets are visible in the full score, pp. 152–164. No tempo is derived from the report’s unreliable onset-tempo estimate.

cues.title: The middle keeps the figure
cues.text: The longer middle section begins in B minor rather than introducing an unrelated tune. Follow how the opening figure survives changing harmonies and alternations between the solo group and the fuller ensemble.
cues.evidence: The score’s large design is A–B–A, with B beginning in B minor. The report marks 1:14 and finds B-minor material across 1:10–1:25, supporting a broad start around 1:14 rather than an exact bar boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: From violinist to organist
cues.text: Bach worked briefly as a violinist at Weimar in 1703 before taking the organist’s post in Arnstadt. The concerto’s treatment of strings and keyboard belongs to a musician whose practical experience included both.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig’s chronology documents both appointments in 1703: https://www.bach-leipzig.de/en/neutral/johann-sebastian-bach-%E2%94%80-chronology

cues.title: Activity without orchestral weight
cues.text: This part of the middle span becomes much quieter, although the small notes remain active. Listen for the difference between the number of attacks and the weight of sound: rapid movement need not mean a full-ensemble climax.
cues.evidence: A strong boundary occurs at 2:28; relative level falls to about −20 dB at 2:30–2:40 while detected attacks remain around 5–6 per second. The analysis does not assign those attacks to an instrument.

cues.title: A nineteenth-century printed score
cues.text: The Bach-Gesellschaft published the Brandenburg Concertos in 1871, edited by Wilhelm Rust. That edition supplies the public-domain score used for this guide; it does not establish which edition the Advent players used.
cues.evidence: BGA volume XIX, edited by Wilhelm Rust, 1871; publication history at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg_Concerto_No._5. The recording source does not identify its performing edition.

cues.title: The opening starts again
cues.text: The returning outer section restores the opening imitations before rebuilding the ensemble texture. Remember the order in which the opening became fuller: the return recovers that process as well as D major.
cues.evidence: The da capo structure is explicit in the written music. Around 3:40 the report shows a level reduction and renewed D-major material, with a boundary at 3:42; the 3:40 placement is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Follow one line through others
cues.text: In the fuller returning passage, choose the triplet figure and follow it through the overlapping parts. The keyboard can provide running detail beneath longer notes elsewhere; a sustained upper note does not mean the counterpoint has stopped.
cues.evidence: BGA pp. 162–164 show sustained upper notes alongside keyboard figuration. This is a general guide to the returning texture, not a claim to have separated the instruments in the audio.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: One documented concert programme
cues.text: The source programme groups this concerto with Brandenburg No. 6 and a flute concerto by C. P. E. Bach. It lists concerts on 10 and 17 February 2008, but does not identify which date supplied this movement’s recording.
cues.evidence: Pandora/Advent programme: https://www.ibiblio.org/pandora/vorbis/chamber_orchestra/MAR-08/readme.html. The track-level date on Commons is February 2008; neither individual concert day is selected as the session date.

cues.title: The running notes settle
cues.text: The final passage resolves the accumulated motion into the D-major close. Listen past the last run to the held ending: the ensemble completes the dance rather than opening another solo episode.
cues.evidence: The score ends in D major with a fermata. The report’s detected attacks fall to 0.2 per second at 4:55 as brightness and level decline; this supports the closing stretch, not an exact release time.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The same subject takes another route
transitions.how: The D-major outer section gives way to a middle span beginning in B minor. Bach retains the dotted start and triplet motion, so the change of harmonic region does not interrupt the dance. Solo and accompanying parts continue to exchange the figure; sequential treatment and keyboard passagework let the middle range farther from the tonic than the opening. Contrast comes from key and texture rather than a new metre.
transitions.evidence: The BGA score gives the ternary design and B-minor beginning of the middle section. The report boundary at 1:14 coincides with a broad change from D-major to B-minor estimates and reduced level; no individual chord is machine-identified.

transitions.title: The solo imitation restores the opening
transitions.how: The middle section’s closing preparation yields to the opening D-major subject. Rather than beginning with a massed orchestral chord, Bach restores the soloist-led imitation: the texture grows again from successive entries. The ripieno strings subsequently rejoin that counterpoint. The return is therefore recognisable both by its harmonic home and by the order in which the opening’s instrumental layers are rebuilt.
transitions.evidence: BGA printed p. 161 begins the written return after the middle cadence; pp. 162–164 restore the outer section. The report drops in level around 3:40, returns to D-major estimates, and marks a boundary at 3:42. The map time is a passage estimate.

source.title: Bach, Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, BWV 1050 — Bach-Gesellschaft full score (1871)
source.locator: III. Allegro, printed pp. 152–164. One ripieno violin part is represented as violins-1; violone as basses. Short opening stages use score proportions, constrained by the report’s 0:12 and 0:26 boundaries; they are provisional, not bar-aligned.

timeline.note: The solo violin begins the imitative subject before the other parts join.
Flute answers the violin; both solo lines continue before the keyboard entry.
The keyboard joins the imitation, supplying its own bass and upper voice.
Ripieno strings add their entries and support to the soloists’ counterpoint.
The middle span alternates solo-group episodes and fuller string support; individual rests are not mapped.
The outer return begins by restoring the opening violin subject.
The flute’s answering entry restores the opening dialogue.
The keyboard returns to the opening imitative texture.
The returning ripieno entries rebuild the full texture towards the D-major close.

composer.epithet: An organist, teacher and church musician who made a bass line, a dance rhythm and a fugue subject carry the same argument.
facts: Family musicians in Eisenach and Ohrdruf; school at Lüneburg; study of German, French and Italian scores
Arnstadt · Mühlhausen · Weimar · Köthen · Thomaskantor in Leipzig, 1723–50
Organ, harpsichord, clavichord and violin; an examiner of organs and a teacher of keyboard players
Cantatas, Passions, the B minor Mass, organ and keyboard cycles, concertos, unaccompanied string music
composer.background:
Bach was born into a family of professional musicians in Eisenach, where his father Johann Ambrosius served as a town musician. The surname already meant a trade: relatives supplied organists, cantors and instrumentalists across Thuringia. His mother died in 1694 and his father in 1695; at ten he went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf who had studied with Pachelbel. Keyboard instruction belonged to that household, alongside school and choir. In 1700 Bach travelled to Lüneburg, where a place in the choir of St Michael’s school gave a boy without substantial means access to an education and a musical library.

The early career was practical and local. After a brief appointment at Weimar, he became organist of the New Church in Arnstadt in 1703, with a recently built instrument to test and play. His duties included working with students, and the town’s records preserve disputes over both his behaviour and his music. In 1705 he obtained leave to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck and stayed away much longer than authorised. Buxtehude’s organ works offered a model in which free passagework, recurring basses and strict counterpoint could occupy the same piece. Bach’s own organ preludes would retain that alternation between improvisatory display and composed argument.
